Chapter 7
Discussion and Conclusion
Chapter abstract. This chapter interprets the results for EST, mass-communication
scholarship, platform design, and future research.
It separates what the evidence
supports from what remains speculative, discusses the epistemicengagement trade-
o, the narrow lter activity, the failure of the semantic block to improve prediction,
and the limits of the sample. It closes with the thesis conclusion and a eld-study
agenda.
7.1
What the Results Mean for EST
This thesis develops EST as an original account of the relationship between platform
architecture, audience evaluation, and epistemic governance. Its contribution com-
bines theory construction, the LOKLOK platform design, a eld questionnaire, and
a separate model-based comparison. These components answer dierent questions.
The survey describes audience judgments in a particular listening setting; the simu-
lation explores the consequences of specied architectural rules. Neither component
should be interpreted as a universal verication of the whole theory.
Table 7.1 states the proposition-level verdicts without collapsing measured,
model-based, and prospective evidence into one status.

Note. H1H7 are dened in Chapter 1. Supported within the model means the specied outcome
equations and ablations imply the pattern; it does not mean a human eld eect has been
estimated. The semantic block is contextual, not the driver of the contrast.
In short, H1 is partially supported but not identied as a eld eect; H2 is
supported within the model; H3 is mixed because reliability is high but structural
validity is not established; H4 is associational; H5 and H6 are exploratory model
checks; and H7 is prospective.
The conclusion therefore keeps the model-based
trade-o as the central nding and the human causal claim as future work.

CHAPTER 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
222
7.1.1
RQ1: Structural Determination
The eld results show that PB scores are positively related to the overall star rat-
ing, broadcaster-rating dimensions, duration, and reported interaction. The model
additionally predicts higher PB and star ratings under the epistemic-rst cong-
uration.
Together, these ndings make architectural inuence a useful research
proposition. However, the eld sample contains no random assignment of architec-
ture and no identied comparison of the relative contributions of architecture and
user characteristics. The strong version of structural dominance in EST-P1 remains
a hypothesis for direct testing, not an estimated result of the correlation analysis.
7.1.2
RQ2: Diversity and the Thermodynamic Analogy
The model reports changes in ECO and correction acceptance and an engagement
trade-o under its specied rules. Those outputs give EST-P2 a concrete model-
based formulation. The eld interactionPB gradient, however, is not a measure-
ment of information entropy, network mixing, or correction dynamics. It cannot
independently demonstrate the thermodynamic analogy. The formal language is
useful insofar as it species an objective and observable predictions; it does not
replace evidence that the real platform follows the specied dynamics.
7.1.3
RQ3: Psychometric Accountability
The supplied R outputs give high internal-consistency coecients, but the factor-t
results do not establish the proposed measurement structure. This is a substantive
nding rather than a detail to conceal behind the sample size. It limits claims about

CHAPTER 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
223
what the BRS and PB aggregates measure. The result is compatible with EST-P3
as a requirement for measurement accountability, while failing to establish H3's
stronger claim that the instruments already satisfy the full validity requirement.
PB combines judgments about condence, diversity, comparative trustion,
structural clarity, and quality. These may covary without being interchangeable.
The very high associations of PB with SV and IQ likewise require examination of
discriminant validity. An audience can regard a broadcast as credible without its
claims being accurate, and an intention to verify is not the same as observed veri-
cation. Consequently, the present scores should describe respondents' evaluations
rather than certify broadcaster competence or student achievement.
7.1.4
RQ4: Integration of the Constructs
The positive pattern of correlations supports studying the constructs together. It
does not distinguish a shared epistemic-quality trait from common-method variation
or overlapping item content. The original Bayesian summary places most predictive
weight on IQ while reporting collinearity. That coecient is therefore an associ-
ation within the specied model, not evidence that IQ is the unique cause of the
other evaluations. A future measurement study should compare plausible alternative
structures and include criteria that do not come from the same response occasion.
7.2
Relation to Mass Communication Scholarship
The thesis places audience evaluation within a platform rather than treating it as
an isolated opinion. Its six-dimensional review connects institutional ltering, at-

CHAPTER 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
224
tention, misinformation diusion, parasocial relationships, measurement, and educa-
tional opportunity. EST integrates these concerns into one proposed design-oriented
framework; the individual literatures remain sources of evidence and competing ex-
planations rather than proofs of the new theory.
The observed starPB correlation suggests convergence between a familiar
summary rating and a multi-item evaluation. This is relevant to mass communi-
cation research because audience metrics frequently compress dierent judgments
into one visible number. The result does not show that the star rating or PB is a
substitute for content analysis. Source credibility, message credibility, and overall
experience must remain distinguishable when interpreting a platform's reputation
display.
The ride setting also matters. The durationPB and interactionPB asso-
ciations may reect opportunity for exposure, content preferences, conversational
involvement, prior interest, or selection into longer journeys. The study does not
identify which explanation dominates. Its contribution is to document those contex-
tual relationships and make them explicit in the framework, rather than generalise
from the journey setting to all university listening or to all forms of social audio. The
radio-specic case is a scope condition, not a claim about social media in general.
The mechanism may transfer, but the instruments, stimuli, and outcome semantics
would require revalidation in text, image, or video settings.

CHAPTER 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
225
7.3
Implications for Platform Design
LOKLOK provides a concrete specication of reputation display, recommendation
constraints, reective prompts, and integrity review. The simulation permits com-
parison of alternative objective functions before deployment. In the reported model,
epistemic-rst settings increase some perceived-quality indicators while reducing raw
engagement. The trade-o index of −.290 is a model-specic summary, not an in-
evitable cost that every platform must pay. Field evaluation must establish whether
the predicted directions and magnitudes survive changes in participants, content,
and implementation.
The BRS display should distinguish an audience-derived evaluation from a
fact-checking judgment. Any uncertainty interval shown to users needs a validated
measurement procedure; attaching an interval to an unreliable or misinterpreted
score does not solve the underlying problem. The same caution applies to modera-
tion and coordination ags: a detector's output should not be presented as certain
misconduct without a suitable review process.
The ndings do not justify using these scores as university credentials or
substitutes for academic assessment.
EST-P4 frames a testable relationship be-
tween platform aordances and communication practices, but the eld study did
not measure veried learning gains or student production quality over time. Ed-
ucational use therefore requires a separate outcome design and safeguards against
popularity-based ranking.

CHAPTER 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
226
7.4
Limitations and Robustness
Sampling and design.
The convenience sample of 52 is drawn from one geo-
graphical and listening context.
The six institutional categories do not make it
representative of Egyptian university students. The design is cross-sectional, and
the respondents were not assigned to architectural conditions. Generalisation and
causal attribution are therefore limited.
Exclusions.
The historical analysis retains 52 records after eight exclu-
sions. Identical answers alone cannot establish duplicate respondents; the all-60
sensitivity analysis preserves the positive associations but changes their magni-
tude (Section 6.4). The original exclusion criterion remains incompletely specied.
Interaction-group sizes range from one to 33, making the lowest group's mean espe-
cially sensitive to a single response. No latent-group comparison is justied by these
descriptive means alone.
Measurement. High alpha coexists with poor factor t. A larger sample
can improve precision but does not automatically correct misspecied constructs.
Self-reported duration and interaction are not automatically behavioural logs. The
supplied outputs do not contain timestamps establishing compliance with the plat-
form's intended momentary-assessment schedule.
Model dependence. The calibrated contrast is a simulation, not a eld
trial.
Its sensitivity sweep explores a nite parameter region rather than every
plausible model. The reported G0 calibration loss also exceeds the stated target
slightly, whereas G1 meets it. Agreement with calibration moments cannot establish

CHAPTER 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
227
the validity of all counterfactual predictions.
Reproducibility. The supplied R summaries support the eld tables and
gures. Cross-le and arithmetic checks establish their consistency, while the new
respondent-level script independently reproduces descriptive statistics, alpha, and
associations. It does not rerun every statistical model. Recomputing the simulation
and Bayesian estimates requires their separate inputs and code. The distinction
between source-output checking and full statistical reproduction is maintained in
Appendix L.
7.5
Recommendations for Further Research
The next empirical stage should rst rene the measurement model and its item
content. It should distinguish audience perceptions, observed engagement, indepen-
dent content-quality judgments, and learning outcomes, rather than combine them
under one label. The required sample size should follow the specic analysis and
outcome, with explicit allowances for clustering, attrition, and repeated measures
where relevant.
A subsequent eld comparison should specify the architectural features being
changed, assignment procedure, exposure period, primary outcomes, exclusion rules,
and analysis before outcome inspection. Repeated observations are needed for H5's
dynamics and H6's scheduling question. H7 requires a direct agent task-performance
or production endpoint rather than a PB or star-rating proxy. Its paired-network
comparison is specied in Section 5.10.1; it is not a completed intervention result.
Human learning remains a separate research question.

CHAPTER 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
228
7.6
Integrated Contribution to Social Media Radio Research
The thesis's distinctive contribution is the connection among a radio-like pro-
gramme, the social circulation surrounding it, and the audience metrics used to
evaluate it. The same episode can be encountered through a host, a friend's post,
a ranked recommendation, or a shared device. These routes may alter the context
of judgment without altering the original audio. EST makes those relationships
explicit as architectural and communicative questions.
This perspective also establishes what the current evidence can contribute.
The questionnaire documents covariation in audience evaluations within one setting.
The simulation expresses a proposed architectural comparison. The new propagation
schematics connect these levels conceptually, but no event logs or network eects
have been added to the empirical results. Keeping these contributions distinct is
more informative than treating all three as independent conrmations of the same
mechanism.
The critical review supports a conditional, not deterministic, interpretation.
Radio-public and podcast-platform studies motivate examining distribution and par-
ticipation (Spinelli & Dann, 2019; Sullivan, 2019). Egyptian audience research estab-
lishes local relevance without making this convenience sample representative (Wajih
& Al-Yamani, 2024). Experimental algorithm research shows that eects can depend
on the direction of a change, prior exposure, and the outcome studied (Gauthier et
al., 2026). EST should explain such variation rather than use architecture as a label
for every possible result.

CHAPTER 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
229
7.6.1
Practical Recommendations Matched to the Evidence
For producers, preserving source links and the context of excerpts is a reasonable
accountability practice, but this study does not quantify its benet. For designers,
labels should distinguish audience approval, moderation status, and independently
reviewed accuracy. For educators, student-production activities require direct as-
sessment of sourcing and reasoning rather than inference from popularity. These are
design implications and evaluation priorities, not established treatment eects.

7.6.2
A Sequenced Research Programme
The rst priority is a complete scoring and measurement record, including language
versions and item behaviour. The next stage is the specied computational fea-
ture comparison with independently keyed appraisal tasks, assessed production, and
recorded network events. Its conclusions concern the model and tested congura-
tion. A separate human study is necessary only for claims about human intervention
eects or learning; human predictive delity also requires held-out human outcomes.

CHAPTER 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
230
This sequence prevents synthetic performance from being interpreted as an already
established change in students' competence.
An informative follow-up should publish predictions that could fail, record
implementation, and compare plausible alternatives.
A rating increase without
accuracy improvement would rene the mechanism toward cue-based evaluation.
No meaningful eect under adequate exposure and precision would challenge the
feature-specic prediction. A diversity improvement without engagement loss would
challenge a universal trade-o claim. These outcomes would advance EST rather
than be treated as reasons to withhold results.
7.6.3
Hallucination as a Measured Phenomenon, Not Only a Bug
The planned agent extension could be asked in review whether its outputs are not
simply the model hallucinating the desired results. That question is anticipated
rather than evaded. In the standard NLP reading, hallucination is a technical fail-
ure to be eliminated. In EST, however, hallucination is not a monolith: the three
measurement types dened in the methodology (Section 5.10, Section 5.10.12) each
point to a distinct process that the design can either guard against as an infras-
tructure error or report as a substantive quantity. Epistemic/factual fabrication is
a task failure against the frozen claim key. Platform-state divergence is an adapter-
contract violation that the validator rejects before it can survive. Persona drift is a
delity quantity that qualitatively anchored design is intended to keep small.
Importantly, a simulation that fabricates a source in defense of a broadcaster
it approves of is simultaneously a model artifact and a computational analogue of
human motivated reasoning and confabulation  phenomena documented across the

CHAPTER 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
231
misinformation literature (Pennycook & Rand, 2021).
Within EST-P1, such an
output is less an embarrassment to be deleted than a measured signature of how
trust can be recruited by reputation signals. It oers a prospective way to relate the
completed rating measures (which record whether audiences report credibility) to
the planned computational extension (which can record whether agents behave as if
reputation entitles claims to belief). The theoretical gain depends on measurement:
the EFI, PSD, and PDS estimators, with a detector self-check, turn an anecdote of
misbehavior into a reported distribution with provenance.
The appropriate epistemic status must be preserved. These are planned in-
terpretive tools for a protocol that has not run; they do not retrot meaning onto
fabricated numbers, and illustrative or hypothetical values are not reported as ex-
ecuted results. Once genuine logs exist, a higher fabrication rate when appraising
claims from apparent high-reputation sources would be interpretable as conrma-
tion bias in the model, not as proof that human students hold that bias. The corre-
sponding defensive claim is therefore disciplined: strict adapter validation and the
measured indicators can show that outputs are not free-oating invention, while the
estimates themselves remain synthetic and model-conditional. Examining agents in
this way also sharpens EST-P4: moderation and integrity tools should distinguish
a detector's probabilistic outputs from veried misconduct  the same caution that
applies to the platform's BRS display in the completed study.

CHAPTER 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
232
7.7
Mixed-Methods Interpretation: RQ5 and RQ6
The qualitative records extend the study beyond whether ratings covary. RQ5 iden-
ties six themes that distinguish reasons for credibility, the attraction of peer voices,
the circumstances of listening, participation conditions, student-lived relevance, and
delivery quality. These are interpretations of short, researcher-recorded cases, not a
representative map of every student experience. Code counts identify corpus cover-
age rather than strength of causal inuence.
For RQ6, the joint display complements the positive interactionPB corre-
lation without contradicting its arithmetic. Some low-interaction cases appreciate
calm, familiarity, or concise content; active feedback can include requests for im-
provement rather than uncomplicated satisfaction. Consequently, treating engage-
ment as the sole quality target would miss some narrated value. At the same time,
praise of audio continuity or a familiar voice is not an independent check of informa-
tional accuracy. A mixed-methods inference must preserve that distinction rather
than use quotations to certify EST.
The separate human-gold validation sharpens that boundary. Three indepen-
dent coders applied the 25-code FGD/self-report codebook with pairwise Cohen's κ
of .762 to .861. The local Qwen 7B pass reached micro-F1 .193 zero-shot and .320
with human-gold examples; the Claude rst pass reached .452. None met the pre-
specied code-level gate for any mechanism code C01 to C05, so E1 to E3 were not
eligible; E1 and E2 were computed as exploratory sensitivity checks and E3 was not
run. The qualitative material therefore remains an assumption audit and a source

CHAPTER 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
233
of candidate design vocabulary, not a calibration target or a test of EST.
A randomized-assignment triangulation (Section 6.12.17) checks the same
contrast for design dependence. The diversity component, the B×C interaction, and
the engagement cost survive all four designs; the BRS component does not. The
interpretation follows: the epistemic-rst trade-o is design-robust inside the model,
but any statement about BRS diusion must be labelled assignment-dependent.
These ndings motivate agent-design dimensions, not deterministic student
types. A prole may include conditional willingness to participate, reasons for trust-
ing a source, time constraints, and preferred content, with uncertainty where the
record is silent. Student-supplied future accounts should rene these anchors. The
planned experiment must then test, rather than assume, that simulated actions re-
semble held-out human behavior. Its computational task outcomes are distinguished
from the completed qualitative analysis and the earlier non-LLM simulation; neither
is retrospectively relabelled as a Student Rating treatment eect.
7.7.1
What the Prototype FGD Adds
The separate FGD synthesis (Section 6.7) suggests that private practice, listening,
collaboration, and publication can represent dierent goals.
Co-hosting, institu-
tional visibility, and interface cues may help or constrain participation. These are
interpretations of overlapping narratives, not additional rider cases or authenticated
transcript ndings. They sharpen questions for EST-P1 and EST-P4 without vali-
dating EST-P3 or testing EST-P2. The supplemental generated analysis adds qual-
ity cautions and follow-up questions, not recovered primary evidence. In particular,
translation errors and unveried attribution do not justify reclassifying its extracts

CHAPTER 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
234
as participant testimony or treating narrative repetition as independent support.
This contribution supports competing mechanisms in a future rule-based
ABM and language-model extension. It cannot supply numerical preference dis-
tributions, factual answer keys, or proof of simulator delity. The shared design
record in Section 5.9 preserves these boundaries so later results can strengthen,
contradict, or leave unresolved the proposed explanations.
7.8
Student Rating and the Meaning of Impact
The central student-focused implication is not that favourable stars prove learning.
The qualitative accounts describe appraisal, participation, and production interests;
the questionnaire records evaluations. Student Rating requires a separate compe-
tence measure. NMLS supplies a published measurement basis for human study. In
the computational extension, however, independent task accuracy is primary and
generated NMLS responses are secondary diagnostics (Section 5.10.12). No human
competence gain follows from a dierence between synthetic congurations.
The existing ndings can motivate and constrain an explanation of impact,
but they do not estimate a Student Rating gain. A model could reproduce PB accu-
rately while failing to reproduce competence or transfer. EST is therefore assessed
proposition by proposition: a credible computational mechanism is not automati-
cally a valid learner measure, and neither establishes a general benet for human
participants. Agreement with a preferred prediction is not a condition for retaining
a result.

CHAPTER 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
235
7.9
The Final Calibrated Upgrade: What It Adds and What
It Does Not
The nal calibrated experiment changes the evidential centre of gravity of the the-
sis. The measured 52-student wave remains the empirical anchor: it supplies the
psychometric relationships, the calibration target, and the substantive reason to
care about epistemic architecture. The upgrade adds a reproducible counterfactual
model that is explicit about its assumptions and its uncertainty.
The strongest
nding is not that the epistemic-rst conguration is universally better. It is that
the conguration produced a large gain in both evaluative and competence-format
Student Ratings while imposing a measurable engagement cost. The trade-o is the
nding that gives EST a concrete empirical target.
Three qualications follow. First, the model contrast is not a eld treatment
eect. The 500 personas are generated from a debiased prior anchored in 52 records;
they are not 500 students. The narrow intervals are a property of the simulation,
not evidence of population precision. Second, the synthetic NMLS prole is a mea-
surement diagnostic, not a validated measure of human media literacy. The human
NMLS remains a prospective instrument, and the competence gain should be read as
a model prediction to be tested. Third, the Hamiltonian diagnostic did not move in
the direction of lower energy in this implementation. The thermodynamic language
therefore remains a formal analogy; the thesis should not present it as a conrmed
law. Reporting this result openly is stronger than suppressing it.
The upgrade also sharpens the design argument. The BRS and ERIC com-

CHAPTER 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
236
ponents account for most of the positive factorial gain, while MORE contributes a
smaller but non-trivial share. The mechanisms are partly substitutable, not purely
additive. The misinformation stress tests show that the governance bundle is inter-
nally coherent under attack. The global sensitivity analysis shows that the model
contrast survives a wide parameter sweep and three network topologies, but that
it is sensitive to a dogmatically skeptical Bayesian prior. That prior sensitivity is
a limitation of the model, not a reason to choose the prior that produces the most
favourable answer.
For platform design, the practical implication is conditional. If a publisher's
objective is raw engagement, the epistemic-rst conguration is not the right bench-
mark. If the objective is epistemic quality, the conguration is a credible candidate,
but its engagement cost must be acknowledged and its human eects must be tested.
The thesis therefore argues for explicit objective functions, not for a universal rank-
ing of platforms. The next study should be a longitudinal, pre-registered deployment
with independent task-performance measures, not another retrospective reinterpre-
tation of the same 52 records.
7.10
Conclusion
The thesis contributes Epistemic Systems Theory, the LOKLOK platform design,
and an exploratory account of social media radio evaluations among university stu-
dents. The eld study reports a PB mean of 5.119, positive associations with ratings
and listening context, high internal-consistency coecients, and limitations in factor-
model t. The separate simulation reports perceived-quality gains and reduced en-

CHAPTER 7. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
237
gagement under an epistemic-rst conguration, conditional on its assumptions. Six
qualitative themes extend these summaries with accounts of credibility, belonging,
contextual value, participation, relevance, and delivery. A separate three-coder val-
idation supports the 25-code FGD/self-report codebook, but no mechanism code
passed the machine-coding gate, so the qualitative layer remains an assumption
audit. The separate FGD synthesis adds four provisional domains and competing
participation designs, not an enlarged eld sample or demonstrated behavioural ef-
fects. Critical review of the supplemental analysis retains this boundary rather than
adopting unsupported claims of transcript recovery or validated mechanisms. The
FGD-informed rule-based comparator and LLM extension remain future tests, not
completed samples. The defensible conclusion is that architecture, audience judg-
ment, and measurement should be studied together, while the strongest EST propo-
sitions remain open to direct empirical testing. The contribution is not weakened by
reporting the measurement problems: doing so implements the accountability that
the theory requires and denes what a stronger subsequent test must establish.
Chapter summary. The discussion argues that EST is a useful design frame-
work but remains unproven. The simulation supports a conditional epistemic
engagement trade-o and identies which mechanisms are active; it does not
support claims about real students or population representativeness. The the-
sis contributes a transparent bridge from theory to a testable design, and it
species the eld study needed to test EST properly.
